name: Adapalene

track.title: Lab & animal
track.line: Rat and rabbit birth-defect studies (oral, high dose)

what.text: Adapalene is a retinoid, a vitamin A-like drug, put on the skin. It binds to retinoic acid receptors in the cell nucleus. The label says it changes how skin cells mature and shed and how the skin's inflammation runs, but that the meaning of these findings for acne is unknown.

In the US, adapalene 0.1% gel is sold over the counter for acne in people 12 and older. Stronger and other forms (0.3% gel, 0.1% cream) are prescription-only. It also comes combined with benzoyl peroxide (Epiduo Forte; and, since May 2026, Differin Epiduo over the counter) and with clindamycin and benzoyl peroxide (Cabtreo).

Very little reaches the blood. In 16 acne patients who put 2 grams of the 0.3% gel on the face, chest and back once a day for 10 days, blood levels were low (mean peak 0.553 ng/mL) and mostly gone 72 hours after the last use.

research.text: Adapalene's US approvals rest on 12-week controlled trials in mild to moderate acne. The current labels describe one trial of the 0.3% and 0.1% gels against a plain gel, and one trial of the stronger adapalene and benzoyl peroxide gel. A 1998 pooled analysis compared it with tretinoin.

research.title: Adapalene gel 0.3% and 0.1% against a plain gel

facts.v: multicenter, controlled trial; adapalene 0.3%, adapalene 0.1% or vehicle (plain) gel once a day
653 people aged 12 to 52 with mild to moderate acne; about half men
share rated clear or almost clear; drop in inflamed and non-inflamed spots

research.found: 21% on 0.3%, 16% on 0.1% and 9% on plain gel were rated clear or almost clear. Total spot counts fell by 45%, 42% and 34%. The plain gel group also improved.

research.meta: USA · label data · Randomized double-blind trial
research.title: Adapalene 0.3% with benzoyl peroxide 2.5% (Epiduo Forte)

facts.v: multicenter, randomized, double-blind; Epiduo Forte, adapalene 0.1% with benzoyl peroxide 2.5%, or vehicle gel
503 people aged 12 to 57 with moderate or severe acne; 54% were 12 to 17
clear or almost clear with a two-grade gain; drop in spot counts

research.found: 33.7% on Epiduo Forte, 27.3% on the weaker combination and 11.0% on vehicle reached the goal. The label says the trial was not designed to compare the two strengths.

research.meta: USA and Europe · 1998 · Pooled analysis of 5 randomized trials
research.title: Adapalene 0.1% gel against tretinoin 0.025% gel (Cunliffe et al.)

facts.v: meta-analysis of five multicenter, randomized, investigator-blind trials
900 people with mild to moderate acne (450 per group)
drop in spot counts; skin tolerance

research.found: The two gels gave similar drops in total spot counts. Adapalene showed a faster early drop at week 1 and better skin tolerance.

src.label: Cunliffe et al., Br J Dermatol

research.text: When given by mouth at high doses (40 and 81 times the human skin exposure), adapalene caused birth defects in rats and rabbits, such as cleft palate and skeletal defects. In a rat cancer study, male rats had more adrenal tumors (pheochromocytoma). Adapalene was not mutagenic in lab tests. This is animal and lab evidence.

us.text: Adapalene is FDA approved for acne. Differin gel 0.1% was approved in 1996 as a prescription drug and switched to over-the-counter sale in 2016. The 0.3% gel and 0.1% cream remain prescription-only. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: approved May 31, 1996 (NDA 020380). FDA switched it from prescription to nonprescription (over-the-counter) sale on July 8, 2016 (supplement S-010). Its Drug Facts label is for acne in people 12 and older.

items.text: Epiduo (adapalene 0.1%, benzoyl peroxide 2.5%) was approved in 2008 and is now discontinued. Epiduo Forte (0.3%/2.5%) was approved July 15, 2015, prescription-only.
On May 22, 2026, FDA approved Differin Epiduo (adapalene 0.1%, benzoyl peroxide 2.5%) as a partial prescription-to-OTC switch, for acne in people 12 and older.

world.lead: Adapalene is an approved medicine in the US, Canada, the EU, Northern Ireland and Australia. Low-strength gel is sold without a prescription in the US and from pharmacists in Australia, but stays prescription-only in Canada. It is not on the WADA Prohibited List.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Adapalene is not named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List, in any class, in or out of competition. The 2027 list does not add it.

side.text: Skin irritation is the main side effect: redness, scaling, dryness and burning or stinging, mostly early in use. Allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. It makes skin more sensitive to sun.

items.text: In the 0.3% gel trial (253 people assessed), scaling (63% in all: 43.5% mild, 18.6% moderate, 1.2% severe) and dryness (62%) were the most common. Most were mild to moderate, started early and eased later. Severe burning or stinging occurred in 3.6%.
Anaphylaxis, angioedema, swelling of the face, eyelids and lips, and itching have been reported after approval, sometimes needing medical treatment.
Avoid sunlight and sunlamps; the OTC label also warns against waxing treated skin and says acne may look worse in the first weeks.

High oral doses caused birth defects in animals. The OTC label says to ask a doctor before use if pregnant. EMA's 2018 review said retinoids put on the skin should not be used in pregnancy or by women planning a baby.

side.text: No hormonal or fertility effects in men are listed on the labels. In rats given high oral doses, fertility in males and females was not affected.

unconfirmed: FDA's approval letters and reviews (accessdata.fda.gov) could not be opened; approval dates come from openFDA Drugs@FDA data and FDA's switch list.
MHRA's own product records could not be read; the UK status comes from EMA's Article 57 data for Northern Ireland.
The lengths of the five trials in the 1998 pooled analysis are not given in the abstract; the full paper was not read.
surprises: The 0.1% gel that has been sold over the counter in the US since 2016 is still prescription-only in Canada, according to Health Canada's database.
In May 2026 FDA also moved an adapalene and benzoyl peroxide gel (Differin Epiduo) to over-the-counter sale.
In the 0.3% gel trial, 9% of people using a plain gel were also rated clear or almost clear at 12 weeks, against 21% on adapalene 0.3%.
